d: How to use grid and table layouts for highly structured user interfaces.
h:
In comparison to UIListLayout, UIGridLayout and UITableLayout allow for more structured and organized layouts. These are most appropriate for interfaces like a shop inventory where each item can be presented in a grid of equally‑sized tiles, or items can be sorted into related rows/columns.

<img src="../assets/ui/ui-objects/UIGridLayout-Example.jpg" />
    <figcaption>UIGridLayout</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure>
<img src="../assets/ui/ui-objects/UITableLayout-Example.jpg" />

Grid layout

UIGridLayout positions sibling GuiObjects in a grid of uniform cells of the same size within their parent container. Cells are added by row or column based on the layout's FillDirection until the next cell doesn't fit, then a new row or column begins. For further control, you can use the FillDirectionMaxCells property to set the maximum number of cells per row or column.

    <img src="../assets/ui/ui-objects/UIGridLayout-Example.jpg" width="500" />

<div class="gcell" markdown="1">
    <img src="../assets/studio/explorer/UIGridLayout.png" width="320" />

By default, UIGridLayout positions sibling GuiObjects in order of their LayoutOrder where lower values go before higher values, and equal values sort depending on the order in which you added them. If you change the layout's SortOrder to SortOrder.Name, siblings sort in alphabetical order.

Once you insert a UIGridLayout, it either overrides or influences the Position and/or Size of all sibling UI objects, so changes to those properties within the Properties window or within a script will not have the normal effect.

UIGridLayout respects any constraints you place on objects within the grid. For example, if an object has a UISizeConstraint with a MinSize property that is higher than the grid's CellSize property, the object will span multiple cells.

Table layout

UITableLayout positions sibling GuiObjects and their children into table format. The default FillDirection of Vertical means that siblings are first positioned into rows, and children of those siblings are positioned horizontally to form columns, such that each cell within a row has the same height and each cell within a column has the same width.

    <img src="../assets/ui/ui-objects/UITableLayout-Example.jpg" width="500" />

<div class="gcell" markdown="1">
    <img src="../assets/studio/explorer/UITableLayout.png" width="320" />

This pattern mimics the standard HTML row/column structure:

<table>
    <tbody>
        <tr> 
            <td>Label 1</td> 
            <td>Label 2</td> 
            <td>Label 3</td> 
        </tr>
        <tr> 
            <td>Label 4</td> 
            <td>Label 5</td> 
            <td>Label 6</td> 
        </tr>
        <tr> 
            <td>Label 7</td> 
            <td>Label 8</td> 
            <td>Label 9</td> 
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

Unless you enable the layout's FillEmptySpaceColumns or FillEmptySpaceRows properties, the size of the sibling GuiObjects determines the dimensions of the cells. For example, a TextLabel of size UDim2.new(0.25, 0, 0.1, 0) will create a table cell of 25% width and 10% height inside the parent container.

Once you insert a UITableLayout, it either overrides or influences the Position and/or Size of all sibling UI objects, so changes to those properties within the Properties window or within a script will not have the normal effect.

UITableLayout respects and is responsive to any UISizeConstraint you place on objects within the table. For example, if an object has a UISizeConstraint with a MinSize property within a header cell, the rest of the cells within the column will be the same size as the header cell.

Note that if the MaxSize property restricts a cell's size from filling the allotted space of a row or column that is wider than the cell, the object aligns to the top‑left of the cell.

kid.simple: Grid and table layouts arrange UI items in neat rows and columns automatically. A `UIGridLayout` makes every item the same size, like squares in a shop inventory. A `UITableLayout` builds a table where each row is an item and the things inside it become columns, like a scoreboard. Both take control of your items' position and size, so you just add items and they fall into place.
kid.analogy: A grid layout is like an ice cube tray: every slot is the same size and fills in order. A table layout is like a spreadsheet with rows and columns.
keyPoints: `UIGridLayout` puts sibling items into same-size cells set by `CellSize`.
Cells fill across (or down) by `FillDirection` until there is no room, then start a new row or column.
`FillDirectionMaxCells` limits how many cells go in each row or column.
Items are sorted by `LayoutOrder` (lowest first) by default, or alphabetically if `SortOrder` is `Name`.
A grid respects size constraints, so an item with a large `UISizeConstraint.MinSize` can take up more than one cell.
`UITableLayout` makes each sibling a row and each child inside that sibling a column cell (when `FillDirection` is Vertical).
Table cells in a row share a height, and cells in a column share a width; `FillEmptySpaceColumns`/`FillEmptySpaceRows` stretch them to fill the space.
Both layouts override the `Position` and `Size` you set on their items.

terms.cell: One slot in a grid or table.
terms.CellSize: The size of every grid cell, as a `UDim2`. `UDim2.fromOffset(100, 100)` makes 100 by 100 pixel squares.
terms.sibling: Objects with the same parent. The layout arranges its siblings.
terms.FillDirectionMaxCells: The most cells allowed in one row (or column). Set to 4 and the fifth item starts a new row.
terms.LayoutOrder: A number used to sort items. Lower numbers come first.
terms.constraint: A rule object like `UISizeConstraint` that limits how big or small something can be.
terms.row / column: A row goes across; a column goes down.

example.title: Build a 4-wide inventory grid
example.place: LocalScript inside a Frame named Inventory (inside a ScreenGui in StarterGui)
example.code:
local inventory = script.Parent

local grid = Instance.new("UIGridLayout")
grid.CellSize = UDim2.fromOffset(80, 80) -- every slot is 80 by 80 pixels
grid.CellPadding = UDim2.fromOffset(6, 6) -- 6 pixels between slots
grid.FillDirectionMaxCells = 4 -- 4 slots per row
grid.SortOrder = Enum.SortOrder.LayoutOrder
grid.Parent = inventory

for i = 1, 10 do
	local slot = Instance.new("TextLabel")
	slot.Text = "Item " .. i
	slot.LayoutOrder = i
	slot.Parent = inventory
end
explain: We add a `UIGridLayout` to the inventory frame.
Each cell is 80 by 80 pixels with 6 pixels of space between cells.
`FillDirectionMaxCells` of 4 makes each row hold at most 4 slots.
We create 10 labels. The grid places them in rows of 4, 4, and 2, in `LayoutOrder` order.

watchOut: Changing an item's `Size` does nothing in a grid; change the grid's `CellSize` instead.
If items do not appear in the order you expect, check each item's `LayoutOrder` and the layout's `SortOrder`.
For a table, put cells inside row objects. Putting labels directly as siblings makes each label its own row.
